Factory frozen vegetables can (although not always) be better for you than some "fresh" vegetables you can buy in the grocery store.

Factory frozen vegetables don't have to worry about transportation time and shelf life so they are often allowed to ripen on the plant providing more overall nutrients in the final product. Produce sent to grocery chains tends to be picked early (before complete ripeness) and allowed to "ripen" on the road/on the shelf. The exception to this is buying local produce in season which is the best (albeit more limited) option.

Boiling can leach some nutrients out of vegetables, particularly if you tend to overcook your vegies. That said, the process of cooking itself (regardless of method) will alter the nutrient mix of the vegetables. Some nutrients will be destroy however others will be released. As with most things balance is always good (eat both raw and cooked fruit and vegatables). As to boiling vs steaming vs frying vs nuking there doesn't seem to be good overall consensus. Different fruits and vegatables react differently to each method.

As to the pre-boiling, the process you are referring to is called blanching. This involves exposing the vegetables to boiling water briefly in order to heat up and denature (destroy) the enzymes that contribute to the decay of the vegatable. The purpose is not to cook the food but to halt the enzymatic action (which can still continue in frozen foods). This preserves the flavour and texture of the vegetable. Not all vegatables need to (or should be) blanched.
